description:
Verified on a FRESH build (the runtime library is include_str!'d, so this needs
a rebuild to test -- see the retracted fz-5xp.65).

A clause in a runtime-library module that calls a function which does not exist:

    fnp digits_value(_s, _acc, 0), do: Kernel.no_such_function("x")

compiles, runs and exits 0 as long as nothing reaches that clause. No
diagnostic, no warning. Reach it and it resolves properly:

    error[resolve/unknown-import]: module `Atom` does not export `from_binary/1`
      --> runtime:String.fz:298:22

WHY IT IS ARGUABLY CORRECT: fz compiles what is DEMANDED. A function nothing
calls is never expanded, so it is never checked, and that is the same property
that makes compile work proportional to the program rather than to the library.
Checking every runtime-library clause eagerly would undo it.

WHY IT STILL COSTS SOMETHING: the runtime library is exactly the code most
likely to name a function that does not exist yet, because it is written
alongside the primitives it needs. Two such calls shipped in this epic's own
work -- `Atom.from_binary/1` and `Kernel.raise/1` (it is `panic/1`) -- and
both were found by accident rather than by the compiler.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT without giving up demand-driven compilation: a check that
runs over the runtime library only, at build time, resolving every callee name
in every clause. The library is fixed at compile time and small; user code keeps
the current behaviour.
title: A call to a function that does not exist is silently accepted when the clause is never reached
